reports.name: Elly De La Cruz
reports.published_report: The contact quality is genuinely elite and the strikeout rate is genuinely a problem, and both things are true at the same time. De La Cruz's 94.8 mph average exit velocity sits at the 100th percentile, his 16.3% barrel rate at the 98th, and yet a 27.5% strikeout rate drags the actual production back toward the mean every time it gets the chance. The .376 xwOBA says the bat-to-ball gap is already costing him — the underlying quality is there for an .881 OPS season with 30 home runs and 29 steals in 643 projected plate appearances, but the ceiling belongs entirely to whoever shows up to chase pitches only 25.7% of the time and not the guy whiffing at 28.0%. If the strikeout rate softens even modestly, you're looking at a perennial MVP candidate at shortstop; if it doesn't, he's a volatile, high-upside regular whose production will always feel a little smaller than his raw tools deserve.

reports.name: Sal Stewart
reports.published_report: A 12.6% barrel rate sitting in the 83rd percentile, paired with an xSLG of .475, explains why the projection lands at 34 home runs even though his average exit velocity and hard-hit rate are both firmly middle-of-the-pack. Stewart barrels the ball at an elite clip by squaring up a narrow band of pitches with unusual precision rather than just mashing everything, and that profile holds up as long as his chase and whiff rates, 31.2% and 27.1% respectively, don't deteriorate against pitchers who attack the zones where he's vulnerable. If they do, the xBA of .259 already signals that the batting average in the projection is doing some optimistic lifting. The floor here is a low-OBP corner masher with real power but limited defensive value; the ceiling, if the barrel rate travels, is a middle-of-the-order corner bat who earns every bit of that projected .814 OPS.

reports.name: James Wood
reports.published_report: A .412 xwOBA with a 19.7% barrel rate both maxing the scale isn't a profile you explain away, but the 28.2% strikeout rate is the one number that keeps this from being a clean star conversation. Wood makes almost no contact with pitches out of the zone, chasing just 21.4% of the time, and his 16.8% walk rate is the reason the strikeouts don't crater the overall line. The contact he does make is almost uniformly hard, with a 58.4% hard-hit rate and 95.2 mph average exit velocity, so the projection's .391 OBP and 32 home runs are the shape you'd expect from a guy this uncompromising at the plate. If pitchers find a way to push the strikeout rate further, the walk rate becomes the load-bearing wall; if it holds, Washington has a middle-of-the-order force in his mid-twenties.

reports.name: Fernando Tatis Jr.

The projection's .285/.355/.462 with 37 stolen bases is essentially the floor if the bat-to-ball stays where it is, and 25 home runs in 717 projected plate appearances reflects a hitter who barrels things consistently enough that the power comes without having to sell out for it. Willits is 18 years old drawing walks at a clip that translates to 12.7 BB%, well above where the average big-league hitter lands, and he's stolen 62 bases this season, so the profile isn't just patience — it moves. reports.name: Kade Anderson
reports.published_report: A 1.1 ERA and a 0.6 WHIP at Double-A aren't numbers that need context — they're the argument. Anderson has struck out 135 batters against 13 walks across 93.3 innings at AA this season, and the command profile translates cleanly: a BB/9 of 2.0 in MLB terms, well below the 3.2 figure where most pitchers land, with a K-BB% that comes out to 21.9% against an average of 13.5%. The whole thing hinges on whether the stuff backs up the control at the highest level, because a left-hander this young who misses this many bats while almost never missing the zone has no obvious developmental ceiling short of a frontline starter. If the stuff softens in the jump, he's still a useful mid-rotation arm, but nothing in this line suggests you should expect softening.

At 21, Walker Jenkins is posting a .417 OBP across those three levels while walking 43 times against only 50 strikeouts in 324 plate appearances, a combination that scouts get excited about precisely because disciplined hitters with real power don't usually need much fixing. The ISO translates to .171 at the MLB equivalent, above what most regulars produce, so the power isn't a minor-league mirage, but his ceiling as an everyday center fielder depends on how much of that contact quality survives a full diet of big-league velocity. If it doesn't hold, you're looking at a useful bench piece; if it does, the Twins have a true regular.
reports.report: Everyday middle-order regular; the walks give him a useful floor through a power dip; the power and patience reinforce each other. reports.name: Michael Harris II
reports.published_report: The xBA sits at .289, 97th percentile, and that gap between what he hits the ball into and what actually lands for hits is the whole tension in this profile. Harris makes loud, consistent contact, 47.3% hard-hit rate, and the .475 xSLG suggests the power projection of 27 home runs is grounded in real contact quality. The problem is discipline: a 45.0% chase rate and 3.5% walk rate are both in the 1st percentile, meaning he gives pitchers an enormous map to work around him, and if the league fully commits to that approach, his actual production could fall well short of what the batted-ball profile deserves. He becomes a .290-hitting, 25-homer outfielder if the contact keeps carrying him despite the zone issues; he becomes a swing-happy second-division regular if pitchers tighten the corners and his chase rate doesn't move.

reports.name: Juan Soto
reports.published_report: The .416 xwOBA tells you everything: this is a bat operating at the very top of the sport right now. Soto chases just 20.8% of pitches and walks at 16.4%, a combination that forces pitchers into uncomfortable counts and then punishes them with a 14.0% barrel rate when they have to come to him. The projection's .395 OBP with a .528 SLG across 485 plate appearances actually undersells the Statcast profile a little, which is worth noting given the 100th-percentile xSLG sits at .580. The one honest limitation in the profile is the sprint speed at 25.7 ft/s — he's a left fielder who runs on the projection's terms, not a center fielder who creates extra value with his legs.

reports.name: Corbin Carroll
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is a quality bat attached to a truly elite body. His 91.8 mph average exit velocity and 12.4% barrel rate both grade out in the top fifth of the league, and that contact quality is what makes a .241 projection feel like a floor rather than a ceiling — the xBA sits at .251, meaning the average should play close to projection but the slug (.473 projected, .451 xSLG) is well-supported by what he's actually doing to the ball. The 27.8% whiff rate is the honest vulnerability; he generates real damage when he connects, but he misses enough that the bat-to-ball profile stays a limiting factor rather than a carrying one. If the strikeout rate holds around 22.7%, the combination of a 29.7 ft/s sprint speed, 23 projected steals, and above-average power gives you an everyday, top-of-the-order centerpiece; if the whiff rate climbs and the contact thins, you've still got one of the most disruptive baserunners in the sport attached to a league-average bat.

reports.name: Tyler Bremner
reports.published_report: The K-BB% across AA & A+ sits at 24%, and the translation puts that at 14.9% in an MLB context, a tick above league average, which is roughly what you'd expect from a back-end starter who misses bats without embarrassing himself in the walk column. A 12.4 K/9 against 3.3 BB/9 across 72.6 innings is the kind of combination that grades well against his peers, but the ERA sitting at 4.3 with a 1.3 WHIP suggests the stuff plays cleaner in counting terms than in results. If the strikeout rate translates and the control holds, he's a fifth starter who earns regular turns; if the walks tick up at the next level, the bullpen is the honest floor and the back-end ceiling shrinks with them.

reports.name: Hagen Smith
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is the whole argument: 13.4 K/9 at AAA, translating to 10.3 against MLB hitters, well clear of the 8.6 MLB-average mark. The problem sits right next to it — 40 walks in 58.3 innings, a 6.2 BB/9 that translates to 5.0 against an MLB average of 3.2, and that gap is what separates a rotation starter from a relief conversion conversation. The K-BB% lands at 19% at AAA because the strikeouts are loud enough to paper over the walks for now, but if that command doesn't sharpen, the 87 punchouts become noise and what's left is a depth arm.

reports.name: Vladimir Guerrero Jr.
reports.published_report: The contact is elite and the power isn't keeping up with it. Guerrero's 13.2% strikeout rate sits in rarefied air for a full-time hitter, and his .285 xBA reflects genuine ball-in-play skill, but a 7.1% barrel rate drags the expected slugging to .407, which is a middling number for a first baseman carrying a roster spot. The projection lands at .263/.336/.366 across a full 627 PA, and that .366 SLG is what happens when contact volume runs well ahead of damage rate: you get on base fine, you don't hurt anyone. The profile works if the barrel rate climbs back toward what his exit velocity and hard-hit rates hint at, because the bat control to capitalize is already there; if it stays at this level, he's a high-average, low-power first baseman who is expensive to roster.

reports.name: Carson Benge
reports.published_report: The xBA sits at .277 against a contact profile that doesn't lean on elite exit velocity, 88.8 mph average and 38.8% hard-hit rate both below the median, which tells you the bat-to-ball skill is doing real work here. His 21.4% whiff rate and 27.9% chase rate are genuinely tidy, and when he makes contact he squares it up cleaner than the raw power numbers suggest, hence an xSLG of .434 running well ahead of what a middling exit velo profile usually produces. The projection translates all of this into a .272/.335/.413 line across 655 plate appearances with 19 home runs and 23 stolen bases, and the speed, 28.6 ft/s at the 83rd percentile, is what makes that a complete offensive profile rather than a just-okay one. The walk rate at 7.5% is the ceiling limiter; if he doesn't grow into better counts, the on-base profile stays solid without becoming a weapon, and he's a high-end second-division regular rather than something more.

reports.name: Liam Doyle
reports.published_report: The strikeout stuff is loud, 130 punchouts across 103 innings at AA, an 11.4 K/9 that translates to 9.1 at the MLB level, but the walk rate is the whole argument. At 4.7 BB/9, the 54 free passes he's issued translate to 4.6 at the big-league level against a 3.2 MLB average, and his K-BB% lands right at 12.9% translated, just below the 13.5% MLB mean despite the swing-and-miss. That gap, elite miss paired with below-average control, is what keeps the ceiling at rotation starter and the floor at depth arm, because if the walks don't tighten, the strikeouts are paying rent on a leaky house. If the command comes, he's a rotation piece in one to two years; if it doesn't, the stuff earns him a bullpen audition and not much else.

reports.name: Gunnar Henderson
reports.published_report: The Statcast card is remarkably flat — xwOBA at .320, xSLG at .397, barrel rate at 7.3%, all hovering right around the median. Hard-hit rate at 43.3% is the one bright spot, suggesting the contact quality isn't dead, just not translating into the shape of damage you'd want from a shortstop with this billing. The projection (.226/.310/.401 across 715 PA) lands him as a slightly-below-average offensive regular who carries his value through positional scarcity, a 9.6% walk rate that keeps the OBP from cratering, and enough speed (28.2 ft/s, 72nd percentile) to steal 11 bases. If the hard contact starts finding gaps instead of gloves and the barrel rate climbs with it, the power profile becomes real; if it doesn't, you're running a .226 hitter at short and hoping the glove (80th percentile OAA) justifies the lineup spot.

reports.name: Luis García Jr.
reports.published_report: The .500 xSLG and 12.7% barrel rate are legitimate second-base power, but García Jr. is chasing at 38.8% and walking at 4.4%, which is about as thin a plate discipline profile as you'll find on a guy this talented. The contact quality grades out top-decile, xBA at .282 and xSLG at .500, yet the walk rate drags the overall xwOBA to .348, good but not great for a bat this loud. If pitchers keep expanding the zone and he keeps biting, the .314 projected OBP is the ceiling on his on-base ability, and the power (.536 projected SLG, 31 projected home runs) carries the whole profile. He's a middle-of-the-order producer as long as the chase rate doesn't climb further; the moment it does, he becomes a streaky bat masquerading as a run producer.

reports.name: Daylen Lile
reports.published_report: The thing that makes this profile work and the thing that could sink it are basically the same pitch: he chases at a 38.0% clip that puts him in the bottom 10% of the league, yet his .444 xSLG suggests the contact he does make carries genuine pop. At 88.6 mph average exit velocity the raw power looks modest, but a 9.4% barrel rate says he finds the barrel on his best swings more consistently than the exit velo implies. Sprint speed at 29.4 ft/s, 94th percentile, turns singles into doubles and projection steals into real ones, and it's the floor-raising tool that keeps a .304 OBP from being a death sentence. If pitchers learn to live on the outer edge and punish that chase rate, he slides toward a useful-but-limited outfield piece; if he tightens the zone even marginally, the speed and barrel rate make him a second-division regular with real counting-stat value.

reports.name: Tanner Bibee

reports.name: Theo Gillen
reports.published_report: The .419 OBP across AA & A+ is what grabs you, but the tension in Theo Gillen's profile is whether the contact quality survives MLB pitching. A .382 BABIP inflating a .315 average is the honest concern, yet a 14% walk rate and 22 home runs across AA & A+ in 533 plate appearances tell you this isn't someone simply riding balls in play — there's genuine strike-zone control and developing power underneath the batting average. The MLB-equivalent translation does knock the strikeout rate above league average and the power back toward ordinary, which is exactly what you'd expect from a 20-year-old still moving through the system, and the 44 stolen bases add a real dimension that survives level changes better than hit tools do. If the walk rate holds and the strikeout rate doesn't balloon further, he's a low-end everyday right fielder; if the contact regresses and the BABIP corrects hard, you're looking at a useful bench bat with speed.

Right now the ceiling is a bench or platoon bat, and the floor is the same.

reports.name: Christian Scott
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the one thing standing between Scott and a reliable mid-rotation role. His 28.0% strikeout rate is genuinely loud, and the contact he allows when hitters do make contact is soft enough, 86.6 mph average exit velocity, that the underlying ERA picture at 3.69 xERA looks credible. If the walks tighten, he's a 3.69-ERA arm eating innings in Queens; if they don't, the 136 strikeouts across 113.9 projected innings become a footnote on a guy who perpetually pitches from behind in counts.

reports.name: David Bednar
reports.published_report: That 39.4% chase rate is the engine, and nearly every other number in the profile flows from it. When hitters are fishing that aggressively outside the zone, a 30.8% whiff rate and a .265 xwOBA follow logically, and the 2.91 xERA confirms the results aren't cosmetic. The profile isn't built on velocity; 96.1 mph is solid but not the reason guys are swinging through air. Thirty-six saves and a 2.62 ERA across 70.4 projected innings is believable as long as the chase rate holds, but if hitters start laying off, the strikeout and contact numbers soften together and this becomes a respectable backend arm rather than a closer posting elite run prevention.

He's not a power threat anymore, a 4.4% barrel rate makes that plain, but the 11.2% walk rate and elite contact give him a floor as a high-OBP table-setter who can still swipe bases, with 36 projected steals in the projection. The whole read hinges on whether that contact skill, detached from real thump, keeps him from becoming a .234 hitter who works counts but can't make pitchers pay.

report_llm.text: Thirty-four home runs across AAA & AA at age 23 is the headline, and the ISO backs it: .275 in the minors, translating to .195 against MLB pitching, well above the .150 MLB average. The strikeout rate is the tension: 26% in the minors becomes 27.2% at the big-league level against a league average of 22.0%, and first base gives him nowhere to hide if the swing-and-miss deepens. The walk rate translates nearly flat to league average at 8.9% against 8.5%, and 29 stolen bases across AAA & AA add a wrinkle that doesn't fit the pure-slugger archetype, but none of that changes what the profile hinges on: whether that power translates. If the ISO holds in the show, he's a useful platoon bat; if the strikeouts climb and the power retreats, the floor is bench depth.

reports.name: Chase Harlan
reports.published_report: The .403 OBP and 13% walk rate across A+ & A are the loud part of this profile. At 19, Chase Harlan is doing real plate discipline work, 51 walks in 396 PA, and the .298/.403/.509 line puts him at the 93rd percentile in OPS among this hitter pool. The translation is where it gets honest: his ISO drops from .211 to .137 MLB-equivalent, below league average, and his strikeout rate lands at 25.4% where the MLB average sits at 22.0, so the power that reads as a weapon at A-ball may arrive as fringe-average at the highest level. If the approach holds and the in-zone contact gains enough quality, he's a second-division regular at third; if the hit tool stalls and the strikeouts inflate further, what remains is a patient bench bat with a narrow role.

reports.name: Nathan Flewelling
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the most interesting thing in this profile, and it might also be the most misleading part. At A+ across 486 plate appearances, Flewelling has drawn 71 walks against 132 strikeouts, a 15% walk rate that translates to roughly 11% at the MLB level, a figure meaningfully ahead of where MLB hitters sit on average, but his 27% strikeout rate at A+ becomes something closer to 30.5% when you run it through the level adjustment, and that's a hard number to build a catcher's career around. The .208 ISO at A+ is loud for a 19-year-old at that level, yet it softens to about .144 in MLB-equivalent terms, which lands right at the league-average power band, meaning the profile that looks like a power-and-patience bat in High-A looks more like a fringe regular once you translate it. Everything here hinges on whether the strikeout rate bends as he climbs; if it doesn't, what's left is a bench catcher with acceptable plate discipline and middling pop.

reports.name: Austin Riley
reports.published_report: The contact problem isn't new, but the current Statcast profile makes it harder to look past. Riley's exit velocity sits at 91.2 mph and his barrel rate is 11.9%, both legitimate, but a 32.1% strikeout rate with a 7.6% walk rate means the hard contact rarely gets to accumulate, and an xBA of .210 suggests the bat-to-ball issue is structural, not luck. The projection's .221/.293/.364 slash across 636 PA is what happens when plus raw power leaks out through swing-and-miss at a near-bottom-of-the-scale clip. If the strikeout rate doesn't come down meaningfully, what's left is a third baseman who hits the ball hard enough to post 18 home runs but not hard enough, often enough, to be more than a bottom-of-the-order problem.

reports.name: Yandy Díaz
reports.published_report: A 14.9% whiff rate puts him in rarefied contact territory, and the .281 xBA backs it up — he's one of the hardest hitters in the league to strike out, and the bat genuinely gets to the ball. The tension is that a 7.2% barrel rate keeps the raw power modest even with 48.2% hard contact, so the production is built on volume of quality contact rather than lift, which is why the projection lands at 24 home runs across 707 plate appearances instead of something bigger. At 35, the whole profile hinges on whether that contact skill holds as bat speed naturally ebbs, because there's no walk rate to carry him (.282 xBA evaporates quickly if pitchers can get him to expand) and 26.1 ft/s sprint speed means the floor is strictly a corner/DH profile. If the bat stays sharp, he's a .290-plus hitter who earns every run he touches; if it slips, the pop was never loud enough to cover for it.

reports.name: Michael McGreevy
reports.published_report: The 5.27 xERA is the honest read on what hitters are actually doing to him. A 17.0% strikeout rate and 20.2% whiff rate both sit near the bottom of the league, and with a 91.9 mph fastball there's no obvious path to manufacturing more swings and misses. What keeps the projection line survivable, a 3.84 ERA across a projected 169.9 innings, is a 6.8% walk rate that's genuinely good, plus whatever soft-contact luck he's been riding, because a 41.6% hard-hit rate is not a contact-management profile. If the walks creep up or the soft-contact distribution normalizes toward what the xwOBA says it should be, you're looking at a back-of-rotation arm who eats innings until the lineup turns over a third time and then gets eaten himself.

reports.name: Manny Machado
reports.published_report: The batting average is a mirage. Machado's xBA sits at .246 against a projected .221, meaning the projection already prices in some bad luck, but the contact quality underneath tells a more functional story: 90.3 mph average exit velocity, a 9.7% barrel rate, and 44.1% hard contact that together describe a hitter who is still generating real damage even if the hit totals don't always reflect it. The 11.6% walk rate is the profile's quiet backbone, keeping the OBP from completely cratering with the average and underwriting those 30 projected home runs as credible production rather than empty counting stats. What you get if all of it holds is a .309 OBP, mid-tier slugger who earns his 685 plate appearances through power and patience rather than average, with plus-tier defense at third base as the floor stabilizer. The sprint speed at 25.2 ft/s flags that he's not covering mistakes with his legs anymore, so if the exit velocity trends down even a tick, the whole offensive package compresses fast.

He's 19 at Double-A, hitting .248 with 10 home runs and 32 walks in 377 plate appearances across AA & A+, which looks like a reasonable foundation until you notice the translated K% sits at 24.3, where major-league pitchers will be happy to leave it. The contact-power combination that works at the minor-league level softens into something closer to organizational depth once you run it through the filter, and the floor here is genuinely a bench or depth role. Everything hinges on whether the raw power in that .17 ISO survives the jump, because if it doesn't translate any better than the moderate-confidence model suggests, there's not enough walk rate, his translated 7.6 BB% trails a league that averages 8.5, or batting average to carry him.

reports.name: Roki Sasaki
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile is a contradiction in cleats: a 97.8 mph fastball and a 29.7% whiff rate sitting against a 10.0% barrel rate and 43.1% hard-hit rate that both land near the bottom of the league. Hitters are missing his stuff but punishing it when they connect, and a 9.4% walk rate is bleeding the leverage out of those strikeouts before they matter. The projection lands at a 4.58 ERA over 127.1 innings, which rhymes with the 4.42 xERA, so there's no reason to expect the surface number to outrun the underlying one. If the walk rate tightens and contact quality firms up, the raw arm at 97.8 mph gives him a real mid-rotation path; if neither moves, he's a back-end innings donor for a Dodgers staff that can afford to carry him while he figures it out.

reports.name: Kody Huff
reports.published_report: The ISO is the thing: .253 at AAA, translating to .187 against big-league pitching, a meaningful step above the .150 MLB norm. That's legitimate thump from a catcher, and paired with a walk rate that translates to 11.7% when the league sits at 8.5%, Kody Huff has real on-base juice to go with the pop. The contact picture is honest, 96 strikeouts across 490 AAA plate appearances, and the MLB-equivalent K% lands right at the league norm, so the floor isn't a swing-and-miss disaster but it isn't a plus-contact profile either. The ceiling is a bench or platoon bat behind the plate, the floor is the same thing, and the whole argument hinges on whether a team decides a catcher with above-average power and patience is worth a roster spot even if he never locks down a starting job.

Wilken has drawn 81 walks in 535 AAA plate appearances, a discipline that translates to 12.4% at the MLB level, but 149 strikeouts in that same sample translates to 27.9% up top, and a .192 average against a .238 BABIP says the contact isn't arriving to compensate. The ISO at AAA is .178, yet the MLB-equivalent reads .144, which is a long way from being a first baseman who earns a roster spot on power alone. Everything hinges on whether the batting average can climb into something functional; if it can't, elite walk rates at 1B don't buy much more than a bench audition.

reports.name: Hayden Alvarez
reports.published_report: The 53 stolen bases are the loudest thing in this profile, and they're also the thing that matters most for whether any of this translates. Across A+ & A, Alvarez is hitting .289/.391/.456 with 75 walks against 109 strikeouts in 551 plate appearances, a contact-and-patience line that looks real at this level but softens considerably when you run it through MLB-equivalent context: the walk rate holds up, translating to 10.2% where MLB average sits at 8.5%, but the ISO drops to .115 and the strikeout rate climbs to 25.2%. The speed is the separator, because without plus run value the power floor is thin and the OBP doesn't carry a lineup spot on its own. Either the speed stays elite and he becomes a table-setter who earns a bench role through his legs, or the bat thins out against better velocity and he's organizational depth.
